claims.text: A qualifying high-entropy solid solution contains at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 atomic percent each.
Superconductivity in the proposed class of HEAs is primarily controlled by average valence electron count.
Average valence electron count tunes electron-phonon coupling through local lattice distortions.
Atomic-size mismatches among the constituent elements produce local lattice distortions and strain fields.
The proposed starting material is an equiatomic or near-equiatomic HEA containing heavy transition metals, including Nb and Ta, together with other elements.
The proposed starting material is a disordered solid solution with a moderate superconducting transition temperature in its as-processed state.
Changing elemental concentrations or making substitutions can raise or lower the alloy's average valence electron count.
Adjusting average valence electron count alters the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Adjusting average valence electron count modifies the phonon spectrum through local lattice strain.
Changes in electronic density of states and the phonon spectrum alter electron-phonon coupling strength.
Electron-phonon coupling strength is critical for superconductivity in the proposed alloy class.
Changing electron-phonon coupling strength produces a corresponding shift in superconducting transition temperature.
Transition temperature will change systematically with average valence electron count.
Transition temperature will correlate with measured local lattice distortion.
Within an unspecified optimal electron-count range, increasing electron count will enhance transition temperature by strengthening electron-phonon coupling.
Departures from the optimal electron-count range may reduce transition temperature through insufficient coupling or enhanced scattering.
The proposed electron-count relationship applies only while the alloys remain single-phase solid solutions.
Phase segregation or ordering invalidates the predicted trend by removing the relevant high-entropy solid-solution character.
